Security Act of 2002, Pub. L. No. 107-296, 116 Stat. 2140, creating a new 
cabinet level domestic security department The new Department of 
Homeland Security would “have the mission of preventing terrorist attacks 
within the United States, reducing the United States vulnerability to

Rept. No. 609 (Pt. I), 107th Cong., 2d Sess. 63 (2002). Toward these ends 
Congress consolidated within the new department i-oughly 17 , 
employees from 22 agencies that previously existed either independently 
or within larger administrative entities. The newly consolidated agencies 
included units with missions as disparate as those of the Federal 
Emergency Management Agency (FEMA, formerly a stand-alone agency 
created through a Carter Administration reorganization plan and 
executive order), the U.S. Secret Service (formerly part of Treasuiy), and 
the enforcement functions of the Immigration and Naturalization Service 
(formerly part of Justice).
So massive an undertaking plainly posed serious questions: Would the 
prospect of improved effectiveness through tighter coordination offset the 
costs to productivity from forcing so many units to re-acclimate to new 
bureaucratic conditions and physical locations? (It is questionable, tor 
example, whether those agencies long ago consolidated into the 
Departments of Transportation and of Energy have yet fuUy to overcome 
their identity conflicts.) Would shifting the emphasis of multi-function 
units towards homeland security diminish their effectiveness in fulfilling 
other functions? (Consider, in this respect, the boating safety, as opposed 
to security, functions of the Coast Guard, or the role of the Customs Service 
in excluding imports that impinge on the intellectual property rights of 
domestic firms, but pose no national security risk.) Could even this degree 
of organizational consohdation produce well-organized antiterrorist 
strategies given that key agencies—^most notably, the Federal Bureau of 
Investigation and the intelligence agencies—^remain under separate and 
historically turf-conscious management?
For his part. President Obama proposed to Congress an ambitious, but 
ultimately unsuccessful proposal to combine the functions and staff of six 
trade- and commerce-related agencies and offices: the Small Business 
AdTninistratinn, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative, the Export- 
Import Bank, the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, and the Trade 
and Development Agency. The consohdation, he argued, would make U.S. 
businesses more competitive and boost exports. Congress was not 
persuaded. In the judgment of pohtical scientist Donald Kettl: ‘What 
essentiaUy happened was that . . . Congress had absolutely no interest in 
surrendering control, and there were so many committees and 
subcommittees with jurisdiction that in the end it just didn t happen. Eric
